content: Representatives from the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO), the International Confederation of Midwives (ICM), the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation were invited to the final Guideline Development Group (GDG) meeting as observers. These organizations are potential implementers of the proposed guideline and have a history of collaboration with the WHO Departments of Sexual and Reproductive Health (SRH) and Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health (MCA) in disseminating and implementing guidelines. Observers do not participate in formulating recommendations. WHO requires experts serving in advisory roles to disclose any circumstances that could lead to actual or perceived conflicts of interest. In line with WHO guidelines for declarations of interest, all GDG members, Evidence Review Group (ERG) members, and other external contributors were asked to declare any competing interests (academic, financial, or other) in writing when invited to participate in the antenatal care (ANC) guideline development process. Each expert completed and signed the standard WHO Declaration of Interest (DOI) form, which was submitted electronically to the responsible technical officer. The WHO Steering Group reviewed all DOI forms before finalizing invitations to experts. If conflicts of interest were declared, the Steering Group assessed their severity and determined whether they could compromise the individual’s ability to make objective judgments about the evidence or recommendations. Findings from DOI statements were managed on a case-by-case basis and communicated to the experts. If a conflict of interest was deemed insignificant, the expert was only required to declare it at the GDG meeting, with no further action taken. A summary of DOI statements and how conflicts were managed is included in Annex 2. To enhance public trust and transparency in WHO meetings involving expert advice on technical norms and standards, the names and brief biographies of individuals considered for participation in the guideline, along with the objectives of relevant meetings, were made public before the first meeting to allow time for public notice and comment. The priority questions and outcomes for the guideline were aligned with those of the 2016 ANC guideline. These were informed by a comprehensive review of existing clinical practice guidelines relevant to routine ANC and a search of the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews for key systematic reviews on ANC. Critical and important outcomes were identified through these reviews and a WHO-commissioned scoping qualitative review of what women want during pregnancy. This review revealed that pregnant women desire a positive pregnancy experience, defined as maintaining physical and sociocultural normality, ensuring a healthy pregnancy and baby, transitioning effectively to positive labor and birth, and achieving positive motherhood. This overarching outcome of a “positive pregnancy experience” became the guiding principle for ANC guideline recommendations. Evidence to support the recommendations was derived from various sources by methodologists working closely with the WHO Steering Group. An updated Cochrane systematic review published by the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group served as the primary source of evidence on the effectiveness of antenatal oral vitamin D supplements. Earlier versions of this review, based on randomized controlled trial (RCT) data assessed and synthesized using standardized Cochrane methodology, supported the original ANC guideline recommendation. The updated RevMan file was customized to reflect key comparisons, GDG-specified subgroup analyses, and outcomes relevant to the ANC guideline. Evidence was evaluated according to standard operating procedures approved by the WHO Steering Group, and evidence profiles (in the form of GRADE tables) were prepared, including assessments of evidence certainty for relevant comparisons. An additional Cochrane review assessed the effects and safety of different vitamin D supplementation regimens, alone or in combination with calcium or other nutrients, during pregnancy. Two qualitative systematic reviews commissioned by WHO for the 2016 guideline development process informed the values, acceptability, and feasibility criteria of the evidence-to-decision (EtD) frameworks. Systematic reviews of cost-effectiveness were identified through PubMed searches. The GRADE approach was used to appraise the certainty of quantitative evidence for each outcome, with ratings of “high,” “moderate,” “low,” or “very low” based on established criteria. Evidence from Cochrane reviews was initially rated as “high certainty” due to its derivation from RCTs but was downgraded based on considerations such as risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision, indirectness, and publication bias. Qualitative evidence was derived from qualitative evidence syntheses (QES) performed for the WHO 2016 ANC guideline and previously appraised using the GRADE-CERQual tool. This tool assesses confidence in QES evidence based on methodological limitations, data adequacy, coherence, and relevance to the review question. The evidence was not re-graded for this updated recommendation. The WHO Steering Group supervised and finalized the preparation of the evidence summary and profile in collaboration with guideline methodologists, using the DECIDE framework. This framework systematically considers research evidence on interventions according to six criteria: effects, values, resources, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. These criteria were populated with research evidence where available, and additional information was described in the “additional considerations” subsections of each criterion. Certainty of the graded evidence on intervention effectiveness was systematically interpreted in EtD frameworks according to Cochrane Effective Practice and Organisation of Care guidance. GDG members and other participants were provided with the evidence summary in advance of the online GDG meeting held on December 4–5, 2019. During the meeting, GDG members reviewed, discussed, and made judgments on the impact of interventions for each EtD criterion under the leadership of the GDG chair. Judgments were summarized before finalizing the recommendation and remarks. The intervention could be recommended, not recommended, or recommended in specific contexts, such as rigorous research, targeted monitoring and evaluation, or another GDG-specified context. Following the GDG meeting, the WHO Steering Group, assisted by a methodologist, drafted a full guideline document to reflect the deliberations and decisions accurately. A preliminary version was sent electronically to participants and the ERG for final review and technical comments. The Steering Group carefully evaluated peer reviewers’ input for inclusion in the guideline document and made revisions as needed. Further modifications after the GDG meetings and peer-review process were limited to correcting factual errors and improving language clarity. The document was then submitted for executive clearance according to established WHO publication procedures. The WHO recommendation on antenatal vitamin D supplementation states that oral vitamin D supplementation is not recommended for all pregnant women to improve maternal and perinatal outcomes. Pregnant women should be encouraged to achieve adequate nutrition through a healthy, balanced diet and refer to guidelines on healthy eating.
